title: Defects, fire-risk escalation and scheduling
audience: Cleaners and supervisors who see defects or recurring deposits in commercial kitchen exhaust systems.
learningOutcomes: Recognise defects such as damaged access panels, persistent seepage and non-operating extraction.
Escalate serious grease accumulation and known fire or system integrity hazards to competent people.
Record recurrence without inventing a maintenance interval or a safety approval.

instruction.heading: Seeing a defect without fixing it
instruction.body: A cleaner working on an exhaust system will see things that are wrong. A panel may be missing its fixings. Grease may be seeping from a joint. The extraction fan may not run when the cooking line is on. A fire-suppression component may be covered, loose or disconnected. Each of these is a defect, and each must be recorded. The cleaner's first duty is not to repair it. Most defects in this system sit in a specialist layer, and the cleaner's scope and eligibility do not cover repair. The cleaner's job is to notice, to make the area safe in the way the site requires, to record what was seen, and to escalate to the people who can decide. This lesson covers how to recognise the defect, how to escalate it and how to record it. It does not cover how to repair it.

instruction.heading: Recognising the signs
instruction.body: The signs that matter fall into a few groups. Access and integrity signs include an access panel that is missing, cracked, held shut with tape, or no longer seals. Leak signs include grease or oily water seeping from a joint, seam or fixing, or a stain that grows between visits. Operating signs include a fan that does not run, makes an unusual noise, or vibrates strongly when it is on, and a canopy that appears to draw poorly, as reported by the kitchen staff. Fire-suppression signs include a component that is covered, damaged, disconnected or obstructed. Heat signs include discolouration or a smell of burning on or near the system. Describe what you see in plain language, with its location and time, and do not guess the cause. The observed sign is the record. The cause is decided by a competent person.

instruction.heading: Escalating serious grease accumulation and integrity hazards
instruction.body: Escalate at once, and do not wait for the end of the shift, where you see a known fire or integrity hazard. That includes heavy grease accumulation that you can see in an accessible area and that the site has not planned to clean, a missing or unsealed access panel where grease is visible nearby, a suppression component that is obstructed or damaged, a fan that has stopped with grease visible on or around it, and any heat sign. Stop the work in the affected area as the site requires, keep people away from the area, and tell the supervisor and the site operator. Where the site's escalation contact or the competent person is named in the site file, call them. The cleaner does not switch equipment off, reset it, open it or cover it unless the site procedure specifically allows that action for that person. NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance identifies fatty residue in hoods and ducting as an ignition risk, which is the reason for escalating grease accumulation without delay.

instruction.heading: Recurrence and scheduling
instruction.body: A defect that comes back is a recurrence. Keep a recurrence log that records each occurrence: the date, the time, the location reference, the observed sign, the action taken, the person told and the response. A log like this lets the owner and the competent person see a pattern that a single visit would not show. The log does not set a maintenance interval, a cleaning frequency or a safety approval. Those decisions belong to the owner and the competent person, who must consider the system, the use, the site's risk assessment and the requirements that apply. In the log, you may write that a recurrence has occurred at a location three times in the period recorded, and recommend that the owner review the schedule. You may not write that the system is safe at a given interval, or that the next clean is due on a particular date unless the owner has set it.

instruction.heading: Writing the escalation record
instruction.body: A good escalation note states what was seen, where, when, who was told, what was done to make the area safe, and what has been left for the competent person. It contains no speculation about the cause and no words such as 'fixed', 'cleared', 'safe' or 'compliant' unless a competent person has written them. Attach the photograph taken under the site's rules and reference it in the note. Keep the note with the job file and send a copy to the owner in the way the site has set. If the response is delayed, follow up in writing and record the follow-up.

procedure: Recognise the sign and describe it in plain language with its location reference and the time.
If the sign is a known fire or system integrity hazard, stop work in the affected area as the site requires and keep people away from it.
Tell the supervisor and the site operator at once. Call the named escalation contact or competent person where the site file names one.
Do not repair, reset, switch off, open or cover the component unless the site procedure specifically allows that action for that person.
Take a photograph under the site's rules, label it, and write the escalation note with what was seen, who was told and what has been left.
Add the occurrence to the recurrence log, with the date, time, location, sign, action and response.
Recommend a review of the schedule where a recurrence appears. Do not set an interval or a safety approval.

workedExamples.situation: A service worker sees an access hatch on the duct held shut with tape, with grease seeping from the edge of the hatch onto the ceiling tile below.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat the seepage and the taped hatch as a defect that needs escalation. Keep the area clear, do not open the hatch or remove the tape, and tell the supervisor and the site operator at once. Record the location, the time, the observed grease seepage and the tape, with a photograph under the site's rules. Note that the duct beyond the hatch was not inspected. Do not describe the cause or the risk level as a conclusion. The competent person decides the next step.

workedExamples.situation: On arrival, the extraction fan above the fryers is not running, and the kitchen staff say it has not run since the morning. There is a layer of grease on the fan housing.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you try to start the fan, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not try to start, reset or repair the fan, and do not touch its electrical connections. Note the non-operation as reported by the staff and as observed, and the grease layer on the housing. Escalate to the site operator and the competent person at once, because a non-operating extraction with visible grease near cooking equipment is a serious sign. Record the time and the people told. Keep the fryers' operation a site decision, not the cleaner's.

workedExamples.situation: This is the third visit in six weeks where grease has been found seeping from the same canister filter housing at the same corner of the hood.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you record the recurrence, and what do you avoid writing?
workedExamples.reasoning: Add each occurrence to the recurrence log with its date, location and response. Summarise the pattern factually: the same location, three times in six weeks. Recommend to the owner that the schedule and the cause are reviewed by the competent person. Do not write a new cleaning interval, a safety approval or a statement that the housing is now safe, and do not describe the cause.

equipmentAndPpe: Defect and escalation note form, with fields for location, sign, time, action and person told.
Recurrence log, kept with the job file for the site.
Camera or phone, used under the site's photography rules.
Site escalation contact list, including the supervisor, the site operator and the competent person.
Barrier or warning sign, where the site requires one to keep people away from an area.
PPE as set by the site and the task risk assessment. Do not enter an area that the site has closed off to attend to a defect.

commonErrors.error: Trying to repair, reset or switch off a component to make the job easier.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, escalate, and record. Act only on instructions that the site procedure gives for that person and that action.

commonErrors.error: Waiting until the end of the shift to report a known fire or integrity hazard.
commonErrors.prevention: Escalate known hazards at once, and record the time you did so.

commonErrors.error: Writing a maintenance interval or a safety approval in the log.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the occurrence and recommend a review. The owner and the competent person set intervals and approvals.

commonErrors.error: Describing the cause of a defect as if it were known.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the sign, its location and time. Leave the cause to the competent person.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance identifies the ignition of fatty residue in hoods and ducting as a risk, and it says that routine cleaning and inspection is an ongoing task. The guidance does not set an interval for any site, and its statements apply to NSW only.
Do not state an interval, a reporting deadline or an approval until the site or the regulator confirms it.
Electrical, fan and fire-suppression components are specialist work. Do not reset, repair, isolate or test them. A cleaner who finds a fault in those components must stop, escalate and record it.
This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority. Completing it does not qualify a cleaner to assess a fire-system defect.

qualityStandard: Each defect in the case study is described in plain language with a location, time and photograph where permitted, and no cause is stated.
Each known fire or integrity hazard in the case study is escalated at once, and no component is reset, repaired, opened or covered by the cleaner.
Each recurrence is entered in the log, and the log contains no interval, approval or safety statement.
documentationEvidence: Defect and escalation note with location, sign, time, action taken, person told and what has been left for the competent person.
Photograph log entry for each defect photographed under the site's rules.
Recurrence log with dated entries for each occurrence and the response received.
Written follow-up, where a response from the site or the competent person has not been received.
summary: Recognise defects, and describe them without guessing their cause.
Escalate known fire or integrity hazards at once, and keep the affected area clear.
Do not repair, reset, open or cover components outside your scope and eligibility.
Record each recurrence, and recommend a review. Do not set an interval or a safety approval.

knowledgeChecks.question: An access hatch is held shut with tape and grease is seeping from it. What is correct?
options: Open the hatch to check what is behind it, then report it
Keep the area clear, do not open or untape the hatch, and escalate at once
Record it as normal wear, and clean the seepage at the end of the shift

knowledgeChecks.question: Who sets the maintenance interval for an exhaust system?
options: The cleaner, based on how dirty the system looks on the day of the clean and the state of the hood
The owner and the competent person, based on the system and the requirements that apply
Whichever interval the last contractor wrote on the job card, since it is already on file

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the purpose of a recurrence log?
options: To set the next cleaning date automatically, so that no one has to decide the interval
To show a pattern of repeated defects so that the owner and the competent person can review them
To prove that the system is compliant with the fire requirements that apply to the whole site
